Hence, grammar boasts that it is the art of speaking correctly, but falsely, since we learn that very thing much better from our mothers or nursemaids than from grammarians. Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi (who were held to be most eloquent), formed their language. The mother Istrina taught the Greek language to Silem, the son of the king of Scythia, Aripithis. It is known that in many provinces where colonies of foreign nations were introduced, the children born always retained the language of their mothers. Hence, Plato and Quintilian determined so felicitously that a suitable nurse should be chosen for boys. Far be it, therefore, that I should transfer this logic of speaking correctly from those women to the grammarians, who, since they profess nothing but grammar alone, know nothing less. # TO THE BENEVOLENT READER, GREETINGS.

*A copy of this commentary was sent to Geneva, so that it might undergo the examination of men who are highly esteemed for both their manifold learning and their supreme sharpness of wit, before it was printed. that some of the Jews fasted twice in every week, namely on the second and fifth days, is evident not only from the example of that Pharisee whose mention is made in Luke, but is also clearly implied in the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate *Bava Kama* <note>(u)</note>. The teachers of the Hebrews in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate *Megillah* <note>(x)</note>, give this reason for this matter: that Moses ascended the mountain on the fifth day of the week to receive the tablets of the Law, and descended on the second day. If anyone compares this with the most celebrated fasts of the fourth and sixth days <note>(*)</note> that are accustomed to be undertaken each week in the Roman Church, he will discover clear indications of Pharisaism. Wherefore these fasts were never in use in the purer Church. For although they object to us the authority of Tertullian <note>(y)</note>, it has long since been refuted by Rigaltius <note>(z)</note> that "stations" <gloss>fasting days</gloss> do not signify fasts there, but those assemblies instituted for the sake of prayer, to which Petavius himself agrees <note>(a)</note>. Indeed, that which they oppose from Epiphanius and Clement of Alexandria <note>(b)</note> has been learnedly discussed by Dallaeus <note>(c)</note>. It remains, therefore, that we still inquire whether this also came to the Hebrews under the name of a fast, when each person abstained from the eating of meat. And I am not far from asserting that, since in Tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>(d)</note>, there is a mention of "fasting from fish." For that perverse opinion had already taken root in the minds of many at that time, as if there were no other way to restrain pleasures and curb lust than by avoiding meats. It was entirely different from what Pythagoras taught <note>(e)</note>, who by his symbol, "do not taste of fish," judged that the eating of fish pertains to luxury and superfluous delights. This error was propagated not only among the Montanists and Tatianists <note>(f)</note>, but the Romanists also received it from the Jews by a quasi-hereditary right. Finally, it must not be omitted that which Gabriel Albaspinaeus <note>(g)</note> reports: that it was once the custom that no one would be greeted with a kiss during the time of a fast, which the *Ordo Romanus* and other writers on rites also confirm. For the custom of the Hebrews, which Maimonides <note>(h)</note> explains, is most similar and closely related to this: "They decrease greetings <note>original: "וממעטין בשאילת"</note>..."

The first of these atlases was originally published in parts, beginning in
1922, and appeared as a complete work in 1925. It has obviously been designed
for a school course involving a careful study of the geography of Poland, other
parts of Europe in less detail, and the rest of the world in outline. The section
dealing with Poland will undoubtedly constitute its chief attraction for non-
Polish geographers, because in addition to the general maps of that country,
and inset maps of all its chief towns, there are folded sheets containing no
fewer than twenty-four small maps dealing with almost every subject of geographical interest—morphology, climate, economic conditions, race, religion,
etc. The whole work is beautifully executed, and a study of it leaves a most
favourable impression of the possibilities of Polish cartography. The representation of the physical geography of Poland is particularly good, and in many
of the distribution maps the choice of colours is admirable. One criticism
must, however, be made, and it is a serious one. The maps are in most cases
too small (the scales vary from 1/3 M to 1/300 M), and the lettering is so fine
that even for a person with fairly good eyesight a. reading-glass is essential.

The second atlas in the above list is a translation of a German school atlas
which was originally compiled by F. Heiderich and W. Schmidt and translated
into Polish. It has since been amplified by T. Radlinski and is now in its sixth
edition. The maps, which have been produced by Hetzee in Vienna, number
forty-five ; of these about half are devoted to Europe, and the remainder are
divided in almost equal proportions between the other continents and the world
asa whole. There are numerous inset maps, some of which, at least, are of
interest. The atlas will, no doubt, prove useful to Polish students, but the
technique shown in its production is not of a high order, and the work as a
whole is inferior to the best German school atlases.

Romer’s atlas, too, is not altogether satisfactory. A few astronomical
diagrams, some charts of the world showing various distributions, several maps
of Poland, and physical and political maps of the continents, constitute the
bulk of the work. The maps of Poland are fairly good, but in general the
draughtsmanship and lithography are not up to the standard of the work
first noticed.

The Statistical Atlas of Poland, of which as yet only two parts have been
received, has as its object a comprehensive survey of the political and economic
activities of the people of that country. It contains much useful information
on a great variety of subjects—for example, population, education, utilization
of the land, mining, banking, language, and religion—and its value is enhanced
by a comparison with the state of affairs in 1913 on the one hand, and with
contemporary conditions in the chief European countries on the other. Most
of the information, it must be admitted, is given in the letterpress ; the maps
are not very illuminating, and consist in the main of circular and rectangular
diagrams placed within the provincial frontiers and indicating for each subject
dealt with the proportion for the province of the total for the whole state.

J. McF.

In the name of the Lord, we begin to write a commentary on Tractate Berakhot.

Rabbi Judah said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of that which is written, "When you take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number, then they shall give every man a ransom for his soul to the Lord, when you number them; that there be no plague among them, when you number them" <note>Exodus 30:12</note>. 
It is taught: Rabbi Judah says, three commandments were the Israelites commanded upon their entry into the land: to appoint a king for themselves, to cut off the seed of Amalek, and to build for themselves the Chosen House <note>The Holy Temple</note>.
Rabbi Nehorai says: This passage was only said regarding the future, that they would stand in them <note>i.e., fulfill them later</note>.
And so it says, "When you take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number."
How is it understood that this "numbering" <term>pekudah</term> <gloss>numbering/command</gloss> is a term of importance? 
It is written here "when you number them" <term>bifkod etam</term>, and it is written there "when you number them."
Just as there it is an importance, so too here it is an importance.
Rav Ashi said: Learn from this that one who wishes to count the Israelites should not count them by the head <note>i.e., by individual tally, which is demeaning</note>.
For it is written, "that there be no plague among them when you number them."
Rav Isaac said: Anyone who counts Israel transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated, "Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor counted" <note>Hosea 2:1</note>.
Rav Nachman bar Isaac said: There are those who say "neither measured nor counted."
It is taught: Rabbi Isaac says, what is the meaning of that which is written, "And he shall give the silver as a ransom for his soul"?
This teaches that each and every one gives half a shekel.
What is the reason? Rav Assi said: In order that they might atone for the deed of the Calf, as it is written, "And he shall give the silver as a ransom for his soul to the Lord when you number them."
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation"? 
"These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel."
Rav Hanina bar Papa said: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And Moses took the tent and pitched it outside the camp"?
This teaches that Moses, our teacher—peace be upon him—would separate himself from the public so that he would be free to engage in Torah and wisdom.
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Whoever engages in Torah for its own sake, the Torah becomes for him a potion of life, as it is stated, "It is a tree of life to those who take hold of it."
And whoever engages in Torah not for its own sake, the Torah becomes for him a potion of death, as it is stated, "My doctrine shall drop as the rain."
Rav said: May the Merciful One save us from such a concept.
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And the Lord spoke unto Moses face to face, as a man speaks unto his friend"?
This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, spoke with Moses gently, in the way that a person speaks with his friend.
Rav Chisda said: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And he would return to the camp, but his servant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent"?
This teaches that Joshua would serve Moses in all his needs and would not move from the House of Study.
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Happy is he who merits to serve the Sages, for through this he merits to learn Torah and fear of Heaven.
Blessed be He who gives strength to the weary and increases power to the powerless.

### §. XX.

We establish that the end which the Jews had proposed to themselves was twofold: one (which you could also call general), that they might observe the custom received among their own people; the other (which was special), that they might harass Christ with the greater torments. Nevertheless, we will leave to each person the judgment of which of the opinions brought forth thus far he wishes to embrace or reject. To us, certainly, this one, which both Casaubon and most of our own people favor, pleases us above the rest. And although we do not dare to tout it as certain and entirely undoubted, we have this firmly persuaded to ourselves, that the other opinions, if they are examined accurately, will labor under their own difficulties likewise, and perhaps more and graver ones than our own.

### §. XXI.

Meanwhile, it remains to be noted that it is added by the Evangelists that Christ refused to drink the wine offered to him. Why this was done is still debated. Next to Kings are the Electors in our Empire, and other estates that rule alone, on account of territorial superiority, concerning which see Wehner in his practical observations under the term <term>Lands-Fürstliche Obrigkeit</term> <gloss>Princely territorial authority</gloss>. II. The Optimates in an Aristocracy and the <term>plousioi</term> <gloss>wealthy</gloss> in the oligarchy of Aristotle’s *Politics*, book 4. These possess the same right to bind successors, whether a transition is made into a completely different form, or whether the rulers have passed away in the course of time, or for any other reason have been moved from their order, and thus others have been substituted in the place of the former; provided that in what has been done, there is no defect, both in the matter itself and in the manner; or that it was not approved by all, or not by the majority, or otherwise where votes are equal and the matter was perhaps not decided. See the Magnificent Lord Boecler on the <term>calculus Minervae</term> <gloss>the vote of Athena/the deciding vote</gloss>, and many others who, transferring these things to a hypothesis in the mixture of the Roman-German Republic, on the occasion of article 5 of the Instrument of Peace, paragraph 19, strive to settle great controversies in the chapter concerning the assemblies of the Empire with a few distinctions.

However, just as we admit the corrupted forms of rulers into the communion of this right here, so too in the Kingdom we wish for domination and Tyranny to be understood entirely. Grotius, book 2, chapter 14 of *The Law of War and Peace*, speaks of these as follows: "The people or true Kings shall not be bound by the contracts of those who have invaded power without right." In book 1, chapter 4, paragraph 15, he adds: "unless they have obtained the right of rule by pact or long possession."

We willingly admit these additions; yet it seemed possible to attempt that such an invader, even without a pact or long possession, as soon as the people whose reins he seized have laid down their arms and are no longer constituted in the defense of their own right, has immediately transferred all rights unto himself; so that not only should his acts with others be held as ratified, but also that the people themselves are stripped of all force against such an invader, and are bound to look upon his acts as if they were performed under royal auspices. See the Magnificent Lord Boecler in his first Grotian dissertation on what the city has done, page 49.
